title: Observer, Pub/Sub, Event Bus, Kotlin Flow, and Mediator
scopeHtml: Scope: Observer, pub/sub, event bus, Kotlin Flow and Mediator with refactors, leaks, and when not to use.

notes.title: Observer: the idea
notes.html:
Observer lets one object (the subject) notify many others (observers) when something changes, without knowing who they are. The subject keeps a list of listeners and calls each when state changes. Observers subscribe and unsubscribe at will.

It removes polling ("did it change yet?") and direct coupling ("when price changes, call chart, call alert, call logger").

+------------------+  1..*  +-------------------+
| Subject          |------->| <<interface>>     |
| - observers      |        | Observer          |
| + subscribe(o)   |        | + onChange(value) |
| + unsubscribe(o) |        +---------+---------+
| + notifyAll()    |                  ^
+------------------+          +-------+--------+
                              |                |
                       PriceChart         AlertService

Before (tight coupling):

class StockTicker {
    private final Chart chart; private final Alerts alerts; private final Logger log;
    void setPrice(double p) {
        chart.draw(p); alerts.check(p); log.write(p);   // knows everyone
    }
}

Adding a fourth consumer means editing StockTicker.

After:

interface PriceObserver { void onPrice(double p); }

class StockTicker {
    private final List<PriceObserver> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
    void subscribe(PriceObserver o)   { observers.add(o); }
    void unsubscribe(PriceObserver o) { observers.remove(o); }
    void setPrice(double p) { for (PriceObserver o : observers) o.onPrice(p); }
}
// ticker.subscribe(p -> chart.draw(p));

CopyOnWriteArrayList lets an observer unsubscribe during notification without a ConcurrentModificationException (cost: each add copies the array, fine for few observers).

Kotlin variant.

class StockTicker {
    private val observers = java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList<(Double) -> Unit>()
    fun subscribe(o: (Double) -> Unit) = observers.add(o)
    fun unsubscribe(o: (Double) -> Unit) = observers.remove(o)
    var price: Double = 0.0
        set(v) { field = v; observers.forEach { it(v) } }
}

Decision gravity. Easy to add, but it changes the control flow into something hard to trace ("who reacts to this?"). Adding observers is reversible; letting the whole app depend on implicit notification chains is not (see event storms below).

Everyday analogy. A YouTube channel: you subscribe, the channel does not know your name, new video goes to all subscribers.

Common interview traps.

  • Notifying while holding a lock: an observer that calls back into the subject can deadlock.
  • Not saying whether notifications are synchronous (on the caller's thread) or asynchronous.
  • Order of notification is usually not guaranteed; do not rely on it.

notes.title: Observer in the real world: Android and Java
notes.html:
API Subject Observer
Android View.setOnClickListener View OnClickListener
Android LiveData LiveData<T> Observer<T>, lifecycle-aware
Android BroadcastReceiver system / app receiver (system-wide variant)
Android ContentObserver content provider observer
Jetpack LifecycleOwner Activity/Fragment LifecycleObserver
RxJava Observable Observer / Subscriber
Java PropertyChangeSupport bean PropertyChangeListener
Java Observable/Observer deprecated since Java 9 prefer PropertyChangeListener, Flow, or Rx

Worked example (LiveData). A ViewModel exposes LiveData<List<Order>>. Fragment observes with viewLifecycleOwner. On rotation, the Fragment view is destroyed and the observer is removed automatically; the new view re-subscribes and receives the latest value immediately (replay of 1). No leak, no manual unsubscribe.

viewModel.orders.observe(viewLifecycleOwner) { adapter.submitList(it) }

The memory leak (classic incident). A long-lived subject (singleton, Application-scoped) holds a strong reference to a short-lived observer (an Activity). After rotation, the old Activity cannot be garbage collected. Symptom: heap grows 5 to 10 MB per rotation, LeakCanary reports "Activity leaked", eventually OutOfMemoryError. Fix: unsubscribe in onDestroy/onStop, use lifecycle-aware observers, or hold WeakReferences.

Everyday analogy. A group chat notification: everyone in the group gets pinged; leave the group and you stop getting them (forget to leave and your phone buzzes forever).

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the unsubscribe path (lapsed listener problem).
  • Observer on the wrong thread: updating UI from a background thread crashes.
  • Treating LiveData as a general event bus: it replays the last value, so one-shot events (navigate, show toast) fire again after rotation.

notes.title: Pub/sub and the event bus
notes.html:
Publish/subscribe separates the two sides even more: publishers send messages to a topic or channel, subscribers listen to topics, and a broker in between delivers. Neither side holds a reference to the other.

Observer Pub/Sub
Coupling subject knows observers (interface) publisher and subscriber unaware of each other
Middleman none broker / bus
Scope in-process, one object in-process or across machines
Delivery synchronous usually usually async, can be durable

In-process event bus. Android developers know GreenRobot EventBus and Otto (now retired). Pros: very decoupled, tiny API. Cons: hidden control flow, hard to test, hard to find who handles an event, no compile-time guarantee someone listens. Most teams moved to StateFlow/SharedFlow or Rx for typed streams.

Across services. Kafka, RabbitMQ, SNS/SQS, Google Pub/Sub. Different guarantees: Kafka keeps messages on disk by offset (replay, ordered per partition); SNS fans out but each subscriber needs its own queue to be durable.

Worked example. An OrderPlaced event at 500 events/s. Email, inventory and analytics each consume it. If email is down for 10 min, it misses 300,000 events with a plain in-memory bus (lost forever). With Kafka (retention 7 days) it resumes from its committed offset and loses nothing. That durability difference is why in-process bus is not a message queue.

Decision gravity. Introducing an event bus is hard to reverse: once 30 handlers react to OrderPlaced, nobody dares change its shape. Treat event schemas like public APIs (versioned, additive changes only).

Everyday analogy. A radio station: it broadcasts on a frequency; whoever tunes in hears it. The station never knows the listeners.

Common interview traps.

  • Using an event bus when a plain method call is clearer. Hidden flow costs debuggability.
  • Assuming exactly-once delivery. In practice it is at-least-once, so handlers must be idempotent.
  • Mixing "event" (a fact that happened) with "command" (a request to do something).

notes.title: Kotlin Flow as a modern Observer
notes.html:
A Kotlin Flow is an observable stream of values over time, built on coroutines. A collector subscribes by calling collect; cancellation unsubscribes automatically when the coroutine dies. Three shapes to know:

Type Hot/cold Replay Typical use
Flow<T> cold: starts per collector none one-off streams (DB query, network)
StateFlow<T> hot latest value, always has one UI state, replaces LiveData
SharedFlow<T> hot configurable (0 default) one-off events, many collectors 
class OrdersViewModel(repo: OrderRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<List<Order>>(emptyList())
    val state: StateFlow<List<Order>> = _state

    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<UiEvent>()       // replay = 0
    val events: SharedFlow<UiEvent> = _events

    fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.value = repo.load()
        _events.emit(UiEvent.Toast("Updated"))
    }
}

// In the Fragment: only collect while at least STARTED
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.state.collect { adapter.submitList(it) }
    }
}

Worked example. StateFlow compares new value with old using equals; setting the same list twice emits once (conflation). A SharedFlow(replay=0) emits to current collectors only, so a toast event is not replayed after rotation (the LiveData bug above). Use SharedFlow or a Channel for one-shot events.

Pitfalls. Collecting in lifecycleScope.launch { } without repeatOnLifecycle keeps collecting in the background (wasted work, crashes touching views). Backpressure: SharedFlow buffer defaults suspend the emitter if a collector is slow; set extraBufferCapacity and onBufferOverflow deliberately.

Decision gravity. Moving from LiveData to StateFlow is a medium, mostly mechanical migration; mixing both in one app is common but doubles concepts.

Everyday analogy. A live scoreboard (StateFlow: always shows the current score) versus a goal announcement over the speakers (SharedFlow: heard only if you were there).

Common interview traps.

  • Explaining StateFlow without mentioning it always has a value and conflates.
  • Collecting a flow with launch only and ignoring lifecycle.
  • Cold vs hot: calling flow {} twice runs the producer twice.

notes.title: Observer refactor: from callbacks to a typed stream
notes.html:
Before (callback hell with manual cleanup):

class Downloader {
    private final List<Listener> listeners = new ArrayList<>();
    interface Listener { void onProgress(int pct); void onDone(File f); void onError(Exception e); }
    void add(Listener l) { listeners.add(l); }
}
// Every screen: implement 3 methods, remember to remove in onDestroy.

After (sealed state + flow):

sealed interface DownloadState {
    data class Progress(val pct: Int) : DownloadState
    data class Done(val file: File) : DownloadState
    data class Error(val cause: Throwable) : DownloadState
}

fun download(url: String): Flow<DownloadState> = flow {
    for (p in 0..100 step 10) { emit(DownloadState.Progress(p)); delay(100) }
    emit(DownloadState.Done(File("a.bin")))
}.catch { emit(DownloadState.Error(it)) }

// Collector gets cleaned automatically on cancel; `when` is exhaustive.

The compiler forces handling all states (when on sealed interface). No remove call; cancellation does it.

When NOT to use Observer.

  • Only one consumer and it is known: call it directly.
  • You need a return value: observers cannot return results to the subject (use Strategy or a function).
  • You need strict ordering or a transaction across consumers: use an explicit orchestrator.
  • High-frequency events (touch move at 120 Hz) with heavy listeners: batch or conflate.

Everyday analogy. Replacing a notebook of "call these three people" with a group broadcast that also keeps the latest status pinned.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing Observer with polling; the point is push, not pull.
  • Loops: A observes B and B observes A, changing state each time = infinite notification loop (a stack overflow in the worst case).

notes.title: Mediator: the idea
notes.html:
Mediator centralises how a set of objects communicate, so they talk to the mediator instead of to each other. With N objects all talking directly, you have up to N(N-1)/2 links (10 objects = 45 links). With a mediator you have N links to the hub.

Before: 5 widgets, each knows others      After: each knows only the mediator
  A--B  A--C  A--D  A--E                     A \
  B--C  B--D  B--E                           B  \
  C--D  C--E   D--E   (10 links)             C ---> [FormMediator]   (5 links)
                                             D  /
                                             E /

Before: a signup form where every widget touches the others.

class CheckBox { Button submit; EditText email; void onChange() { submit.enabled = checked && !email.text.isEmpty(); } }
class EditText { Button submit; CheckBox terms; void onChange() { submit.enabled = !text.isEmpty() && terms.checked; } }

The rule "submit is enabled when email filled and terms checked" is smeared over several classes.

After:

interface FormMediator { void changed(Widget source); }

class SignupMediator implements FormMediator {
    EditText email; CheckBox terms; Button submit;
    public void changed(Widget src) {
        submit.setEnabled(!email.getText().isEmpty() && terms.isChecked());
    }
}
abstract class Widget { protected FormMediator med; void notifyChange() { med.changed(this); } }

Widgets only call med.changed(this). The rule lives in one place and can be tested without any UI.

Kotlin variant.

class SignupMediator {
    var email = ""; var terms = false
    val submitEnabled get() = email.isNotBlank() && terms
}

Real Android: this logic lives in a ViewModel (a mediator between UI widgets and the model), exposing one StateFlow<FormState>.

Real examples.

  • Android ViewModel / MVP Presenter: mediates between View and Model.
  • java.util.Timer coordinates tasks; Swing ButtonGroup.
  • Air traffic control tower: planes talk to the tower, not each other. Chat room server: users post to the room, not to each other.
  • MediatR (.NET) for in-process request/handler dispatch; Spring ApplicationEventPublisher.

Observer vs Mediator. Observer is one-to-many broadcast with no logic ("something changed"). Mediator holds coordination logic ("when A changes, enable B and refresh C"). A mediator is often built with observers underneath.

When NOT to use Mediator.

  • Two or three objects: direct calls are clearer.
  • The mediator grows into a "god object" with 2,000 lines knowing everything. Split by feature or use several small mediators.

Decision gravity. Introducing a mediator is a moderate, local refactor. The cost is hidden: you moved the coupling into the mediator, you did not remove it. Reversible if kept small.

Everyday analogy. Air traffic control: 50 planes never talk to each other, all go through the tower.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling any ViewModel a "Mediator". It is one role of it; say what it coordinates.
  • Describing Mediator as "Observer". Observer broadcasts; Mediator decides.
  • God-object risk not mentioned.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Observer: subject notifies subscribed observers; removes polling and hard-coded callers. Decide sync vs async, and always unsubscribe.
  • Android: LiveData, LifecycleObserver, click listeners. Leaks happen when a long-lived subject keeps a short-lived observer (LeakCanary shows it).
  • Pub/sub adds a broker so neither side knows the other; in-process bus is not durable, Kafka-style brokers are. Handlers must be idempotent (at-least-once).
  • Kotlin Flow: cold Flow, hot StateFlow (state, conflated, always a value), SharedFlow (events). Use repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) in UI.
  • Mediator centralises communication among many objects (N links instead of N^2) and holds the coordination rule; ViewModel/Presenter is the Android example. Avoid god-mediators.
  • Do not use these for single known consumers, when a return value is needed, or when strict ordering matters.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Observer pattern, and what are its roles?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Baseline: can you explain one-to-many notification and the coupling it removes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A subject keeps a list of observers and notifies them when its state changes. The subject only knows an Observer interface, so it does not depend on who listens. New listener means subscribe; the subject is not edited.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Roles: Subject (register, unregister, notify), Observer (onChanged), concrete observers. Push model sends the data; pull model sends a signal and observers read state. Key risks: memory leaks (forgotten unsubscribe), notification order assumptions, modification during iteration, slow observers blocking the subject.

Subject --notify--> Observer A
        --notify--> Observer B

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface PriceListener { void onPrice(String sym, double p); }
class PriceFeed {
    private final List<PriceListener> ls = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
    void subscribe(PriceListener l) { ls.add(l); }
    void unsubscribe(PriceListener l) { ls.remove(l); }
    void publish(String s, double p) { for (PriceListener l : ls) l.onPrice(s, p); }
}
fun interface PriceListener { fun onPrice(sym: String, p: Double) }
class PriceFeed {
    private val ls = java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList<PriceListener>()
    fun subscribe(l: PriceListener) { ls.add(l) }
    fun unsubscribe(l: PriceListener) { ls.remove(l) }
    fun publish(s: String, p: Double) = ls.forEach { it.onPrice(s, p) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Never unsubscribing (lapsed listener leak).
  • Assuming a fixed notification order.
  • Letting an exception in one observer stop the rest.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Push vs pull? -> Push sends data (simple, may over-send); pull sends a signal and observers query.
  2. Why CopyOnWriteArrayList? -> Safe iteration while observers add or remove themselves.
  3. Observer vs Strategy? -> Observer is one-to-many notification; Strategy is one chosen algorithm.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior names leaks, ordering, reentrancy and threading of callbacks unprompted.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Android LiveData and View.OnClickListener are Observer; leaked listeners are a classic memory leak source.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The commonly blurred distinction: direct reference versus broker.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In Observer, observers register directly with the subject, so they know each other's type. In pub/sub a broker (topic or event bus) sits between publishers and subscribers; neither knows the other and subscribers filter by topic or event type. Pub/sub decouples more, but makes flow harder to trace.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect Observer Pub/sub / event bus
Link subject holds observers broker holds subscriptions
Knowledge observer knows subject only the event type
Typical scope in one object graph app or system wide
Debuggability call stack shows path "who handled this?" needs tooling
Delivery usually sync often async, can be durable

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a global bus for what is a local callback.
  • Treating a message broker (Kafka) as the same thing as an in-process bus: delivery guarantees differ.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do teams abandon event buses? -> Hidden coupling, untraceable flows, ordering surprises.
  2. Sync or async dispatch? -> Async avoids blocking publishers but loses the call stack and ordering.
  3. When is a bus appropriate? -> Truly decoupled modules, fire-and-forget notifications.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions debuggability and typed events over stringly-typed topics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A global bus with 70 event types made a bug unfindable until events were typed and logged.

questions.promptHtml: Compare Flow, StateFlow, SharedFlow and LiveData as observer mechanisms.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests modern Android/Kotlin practice and hot vs cold understanding.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A plain Flow is cold: each collector starts its own producer. StateFlow is hot, always holds a current value and replays it to new collectors, good for UI state. SharedFlow is hot with configurable replay, good for one-off events. LiveData is lifecycle-aware and Android-only; Flow plus repeatOnLifecycle replaces it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Observer on top of coroutines gives you operators (map, debounce), backpressure choices (buffer, conflate), and cancellation tied to scope. StateFlow conflates and compares by equality, so identical consecutive values are dropped.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Kotlin

class VM : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(UiState())
    val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state.asStateFlow()
    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<Event>()   // no replay
    val events = _events.asSharedFlow()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using StateFlow for one-shot events (a replayed value fires again after rotation).
  • Collecting in lifecycleScope.launch without repeatOnLifecycle, so it keeps running in background.
  • Expecting StateFlow to emit duplicates.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does StateFlow have an initial value? -> It always represents current state.
  2. Hot vs cold? -> Hot producers run independent of collectors.
  3. How do you avoid dropped events? -> SharedFlow with buffer or a Channel for exactly-once.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior picks the type by semantics (state vs event) and names lifecycle collection.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "show toast" StateFlow replayed the toast after every rotation.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Mediator pattern and how is it different from Observer?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many-to-many coordination and where the logic lives.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A mediator is a central object that coordinates a group of colleagues so they do not reference each other directly. N-to-N links become N-to-1. Observer is one-way notification with no coordination logic; a mediator holds the interaction rules (when A changes, enable B and hide C).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example: a form where the country dropdown, state dropdown and submit button all react to each other; a FormMediator owns the rules. Chat room: users send to the room, the room routes. Risk: the mediator becomes a god object.

Colleague A \
Colleague B -> Mediator (rules)
Colleague C /

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Letting the mediator absorb all business logic.
  • Using it for two objects (a direct call is clearer).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you see it in Android? -> A presenter/ViewModel coordinating views, FragmentManager mediating fragments.
  2. How do you stop god mediators? -> Split by sub-flow, one mediator per interaction cluster.
  3. Mediator vs event bus? -> Mediator is explicit and scoped; a bus is global and implicit.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior calls out the god-object risk and where the line to a controller sits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout form with 15 inter-dependent fields became testable after rules moved into one mediator class.

questions.contextHtml:
Memory profile shows HomeActivity instances growing after each rotation (heap dump: 14 instances retained, 9 MB each). Code:

object LocationBus {
    private val listeners = mutableListOf<(Location) -> Unit>()
    fun register(l: (Location) -> Unit) { listeners.add(l) }
}
class HomeActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(b: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(b)
        LocationBus.register { loc -> label.text = loc.toString() }   // captures this
    }
}

LeakCanary trace: LocationBus.listeners -> lambda -> HomeActivity.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Call System.gc()" or "null the label"; misses that the static registry owns the lambda.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the bus a singleton? Do other callers register the same way?
  2. Immediate mitigation: ship an unregister in onDestroy as a hotfix.
  3. Root cause: a long-lived singleton holds a strong reference to a lambda that captures the short-lived Activity ("lapsed listener").
  4. Fix: tie registration to lifecycle.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class LocationBus {
    private static final List<Consumer<Location>> ls = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
    static Runnable register(Consumer<Location> l) { ls.add(l); return () -> ls.remove(l); }
}
// In Activity: private Runnable undo; onStart: undo = LocationBus.register(...); onStop: undo.run();
override fun onStart() { super.onStart(); undo = LocationBus.register { label.text = it.toString() } }
override fun onStop() { undo?.invoke(); super.onStop() }
  1. Better: expose a Flow<Location> and collect with repeatOnLifecycle, so cancellation is automatic.
  2. Prevention: LeakCanary in debug builds; rule that register returns a handle.
  3. Trade-offs: weak references hide the leak but can drop listeners silently; I prefer explicit lifecycle.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Register in onCreate, unregister in onDestroy? -> Mismatched with lifecycle if the view is recreated; use start/stop.
  • Fragments? -> Use viewLifecycleOwner.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An "unused" analytics listener retained three screens of bitmaps and caused OOM crashes on low-memory devices.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames GC.
  • Hire: identifies static registry plus unregister.
  • Strong hire: lifecycle-bound Flow and leak detection in CI.

questions.contextHtml:
Intermittent crash in production: ConcurrentModificationException at ArrayList$Itr.next inside EventSource.fire. Code:

class EventSource {
    private final List<Listener> ls = new ArrayList<>();
    void add(Listener l) { ls.add(l); }
    void remove(Listener l) { ls.remove(l); }
    void fire(Event e) { for (Listener l : ls) l.on(e); }
}
// a one-shot listener removes itself inside on()
questions.promptHtml: Why does it crash, and what are the options?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap in try/catch." The listener list is still corrupt-prone across threads.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Single-threaded or multi-threaded? Is a removed listener allowed to still receive the current event?
  2. Immediate mitigation: copy before iterating: for (Listener l : new ArrayList<>(ls)).
  3. Root cause: removing from the list during iteration (same thread) or another thread mutating it (ArrayList is not thread-safe).
  4. Options: CopyOnWriteArrayList (snapshot iteration, cheap when reads dominate and listeners change rarely); copy-on-fire; a pending-removal queue applied after dispatch.
  5. Semantics to document: a listener removed during dispatch may still see the current event; exceptions in one listener must not stop the rest, so wrap each call in try/catch and log.
  6. Prevention: a unit test with a self-removing listener and a concurrent add/remove test.
  7. Trade-offs: COW is O(n) per mutation; with thousands of churning listeners use a concurrent set plus snapshot.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Listener adds another listener inside on? -> Snapshot means it is not called for the current event.
  • Deadlock? -> Never call listeners while holding the subject's lock.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A one-shot listener pattern crashed only under load when two events overlapped; a snapshot dispatch fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swallows the exception.
  • Hire: COW or copy.
  • Strong hire: semantics, isolation of listener exceptions, tests, lock rule.

questions.contextHtml: A Downloader takes onProgress, onSuccess, onError callbacks. Callers nest them, miss error paths, and forget to detach in onDestroy. Three screens show the same download.
questions.promptHtml: Refactor to a typed stream and say what you gain and risk.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use RxJava" without modelling states.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should multiple screens share one download? Replay the last state to late subscribers?
  2. Model the states as a sealed type:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
sealed interface DownloadState {
    record Progress(int pct) implements DownloadState {}
    record Done(File f) implements DownloadState {}
    record Failed(Throwable t) implements DownloadState {}
}
sealed interface DownloadState {
    data class Progress(val pct: Int) : DownloadState
    data class Done(val f: File) : DownloadState
    data class Failed(val t: Throwable) : DownloadState
}
fun download(url: String): StateFlow<DownloadState> = /* shared in a scope */ TODO()
  1. Gains: exhaustive when, one subscription mechanism, replay of the latest state to late screens, cancellation by scope, no forgotten detach.
  2. Risks: the stream must be shared (stateIn) or each collector starts its own download; terminal states need care (a Done state replays after rotation).
  3. Migration: keep the old callback API as an adapter built on the stream for one release.
  4. Prevention: a test that collects Progress, Done and Failed in order.
  5. Trade-offs: if there is exactly one caller and one result, a suspend function returning a result is simpler than a stream.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cancel the download when the last screen leaves? -> SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000).
  • Java callers? -> Provide a CompletableFuture or listener adapter.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Three screens triggered three downloads of the same file until the flow was shared once in the repository.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swaps libraries only.
  • Hire: sealed states plus stream.
  • Strong hire: sharing, replay semantics, migration adapter, simpler-alternative check.

questions.contextHtml: OrderService.place() currently calls emailService.send() and inventory.reserve() directly. Product now wants an SMS, a Slack alert for big orders, and an analytics event.
questions.promptHtml: What do you change so that adding the fourth channel later touches no existing class? What do you refuse to put behind the observer?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Append three more direct calls to place().

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must inventory reservation succeed atomically with placing? Can notifications be eventually delivered? Who owns retries?
  2. Approach: publish an OrderPlaced event; email, SMS, Slack, analytics are subscribers.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
record OrderPlaced(String id, double total) {}
interface OrderListener { void on(OrderPlaced e); }
// OrderService.place(): save(o); listeners.forEach(l -> safeCall(l, e));
data class OrderPlaced(val id: String, val total: Double)
fun interface OrderListener { fun on(e: OrderPlaced) }
  1. What stays direct: inventory reservation. It is part of the transaction and failure must abort the order; observers are for side effects that may fail independently.
  2. Failure isolation: each listener wrapped; a Slack outage must not fail checkout; for must-deliver channels use an outbox plus queue rather than in-process observers.
  3. Prevention: tests that a failing listener does not break place().
  4. Trade-offs: control flow is now implicit; log each dispatch.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Listener is slow? -> Dispatch async on an executor.
  • Need ordering (email after SMS)? -> Then it is a workflow, not an observer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A Slack timeout of 30s blocked checkout for everyone until notifications went async.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more direct calls.
  • Hire: event plus listeners.
  • Strong hire: transactional boundary, failure isolation, outbox mention.

questions.contextHtml: An in-app event bus has 70 event types. After a release, the "Cart" badge shows stale counts in 3% of sessions. Logs show: CartUpdated received by 5 subscribers; handler order: Badge, Pricing, Badge. The Badge subscribes twice (once in onCreate, once in onResume). A PriceChanged handler posts CartUpdated again.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix, and say whether you keep the bus.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a delay before the badge reads." Hides ordering coupling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Sync or async bus? Which thread delivers? Can I log event-chain depth?
  2. Immediate mitigation: make register idempotent (ignore duplicate subscribers); roll back the release if needed.
  3. Hypotheses: duplicate subscription; event cascade (CartUpdated -> PriceChanged -> CartUpdated); handlers assuming order; stale state captured.
  4. Verify: log with a correlation id and depth; count subscribers per type.
  5. Root cause: duplicate registration plus a cycle between two events with order-dependent handlers.
  6. Fix: idempotent register, break the cycle (derive price from cart state instead of re-posting), make the badge read state, not event payload.
  7. Prevention: typed events, a debug-mode dispatch trace, a rule that handlers must not post their own trigger events.
  8. Trade-offs: I'd keep the bus for truly decoupled modules but move cart state into a StateFlow owner; replacing the bus wholesale is a large risk.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cycle detection at runtime? -> Depth counter that throws in debug builds.
  • Process death? -> Events are not state; rebuild from the source of truth.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" bus grew to 70 events and nobody could answer who consumed which; a dispatch trace revealed two dead subscribers and one cycle.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds delays.
  • Hire: finds duplicate subscription and cycle.
  • Strong hire: state ownership, tracing, bounded bus use.

questions.contextHtml:
A screen consumes viewModel.state and viewModel.events. QA reports: after rotation the "Saved" snackbar appears again; the app also drains battery because location updates continue after the app goes to background. Code:

lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewModel.state.collect { render(it) }
    viewModel.events.collect { show(it) }     // never reached
}

events is a MutableStateFlow<Event?>.
questions.promptHtml: List every bug and the corrected design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Fixes only the snackbar by setting the event to null.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should the event be delivered if nobody is collecting? Is there more than one collector?
  2. Bugs: (a) the first collect suspends forever, so the second never runs; (b) a StateFlow replays its current value to new collectors, so events re-fire after rotation; (c) collection is not lifecycle-aware, so it runs while stopped.
  3. Fix:
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        launch { viewModel.state.collect { render(it) } }
        launch { viewModel.events.collect { show(it) } }
    }
}
// ViewModel: private val _events = Channel<Event>(Channel.BUFFERED); val events = _events.receiveAsFlow()
  1. Why a Channel: exactly-once consumption and buffering while the UI is stopped; a SharedFlow without replay would drop events while stopped.
  2. Prevention: a test that rotates and asserts no replay; lint for launch plus collect outside repeatOnLifecycle.
  3. Trade-offs: better still is modelling the snackbar as state with a consumed flag, which survives process recreation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Multiple consumers of the event? -> Channel gives one consumer; use SharedFlow with replay 0 and accept drops, or model as state.
  • flowWithLifecycle? -> Equivalent for one flow.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payment "success" dialog replayed after rotation and customers retried the payment.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sets event to null.
  • Hire: spots suspension, replay, lifecycle.
  • Strong hire: Channel vs SharedFlow vs state reasoning.

questions.contextHtml:
A price feed publishes 5,000 updates/s synchronously on its single thread. One subscriber writes to a database (8 ms per call). Feed lag reaches 40 s; a thread dump shows the feed thread BLOCKED on Portfolio.lock held by a listener thread waiting on PriceFeed.lock.

"feed" waiting to lock Portfolio@3a (held by "ui")
"ui"   waiting to lock PriceFeed@1f (held by "feed")

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase thread pool size."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is dropping or coalescing updates acceptable? Which subscribers must be in order?
  2. Immediate mitigation: disable the DB subscriber or put it behind a bounded queue.
  3. Hypotheses: synchronous dispatch ties publisher speed to the slowest subscriber (8 ms x 5000 = 40 s of work per second); lock-order inversion between the subject lock and the listener lock.
  4. Verify: jstack shows the cycle; per-listener timing metrics.
  5. Fix: never call listeners while holding the subject's lock (snapshot, release, then notify); give slow subscribers their own bounded queue and worker with a policy (drop oldest or conflate to latest per symbol); batch DB writes.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void publish(Tick t) {
    List<Listener> snap;
    synchronized (this) { snap = List.copyOf(listeners); }   // lock released before callbacks
    for (Listener l : snap) l.on(t);
}
fun publish(t: Tick) {
    val snap = synchronized(this) { listeners.toList() }
    snap.forEach { it.on(t) }
}
  1. Prevention: per-subscriber lag metrics and alarms; a rule that listeners must be quick.
  2. Trade-offs: async queues lose the call stack and ordering across subscribers; conflation loses intermediate ticks (acceptable for UI, not for ledgers).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Must not lose ticks for audit? -> Durable log or queue; not an in-process observer.
  • Backpressure? -> Bounded queue with explicit overflow policy.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A dashboard listener doing blocking I/O silently throttled the whole feed until a conflating queue was added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more threads.
  • Hire: lock-free callbacks and async slow listeners.
  • Strong hire: overflow policy, conflation vs durability, metrics.

questions.contextHtml: A flight-search form has 12 widgets (origin, destination, dates, one-way toggle, passengers, promo, submit...). Every widget calls other widgets directly; a recent change to "one-way" broke the return-date validation and nobody can predict side effects. Unit tests need a full screen.
questions.promptHtml: Model it with a Mediator, show the shape, and explain how you keep the mediator from becoming a god class and how you test it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: One 1,200-line FormController with every rule.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which rules are pure validation vs UI visibility? Are widgets reused elsewhere?
  2. Approach: widgets implement Colleague, report changes to FormMediator.notify(sender, event); the mediator updates others via small interfaces. Better: the mediator owns a plain FormState and widgets render from it.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface FormMediator { void changed(Widget w, String event); }
class FlightFormMediator implements FormMediator {
    private Toggle oneWay; private DatePicker ret; private Button submit;
    public void changed(Widget w, String ev) {
        if (w == oneWay) ret.setVisible(!oneWay.isOn());
        submit.setEnabled(valid());
    }
    private boolean valid() { return true; }
}
interface FormMediator { fun changed(w: Widget, event: String) }
class FlightFormMediator(private val oneWay: Toggle, private val ret: DatePicker,
                         private val submit: Button) : FormMediator {
    override fun changed(w: Widget, event: String) {
        if (w === oneWay) ret.visible = !oneWay.isOn
        submit.enabled = valid()
    }
    private fun valid() = true
}
  1. Avoiding a god class: pure validation goes into separate rule classes; mediator only wires events to rules; one mediator per section if 12 widgets split into logical groups.
  2. Testing: inject fake widgets (interfaces); fire changed and assert states; with the state-based version, test reduce(state, event) -> state with no UI at all.
  3. Trade-offs: the mediator centralises coupling; for two widgets a direct call is clearer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Reuse widgets elsewhere? -> They only know the mediator interface, so yes.
  • Move to Compose? -> State hoisting is the same idea: state owner plus events.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving rules into a state reducer let QA write 40 table tests and the one-way regression never returned.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: god controller.
  • Hire: mediator plus colleague interfaces.
  • Strong hire: state reducer, rule split, test seams, scope judgement.
